Volume Changed. Lethality Didn’t Follow.

NYPD Shooting Incident Data, 2006-present

Mo

2026-10-06

Note: install.packages("tidyverse") is deliberately not in this document. Install once from the console; the Rmd only loads libraries so that knitting is fast and side-effect free.

Step 1: Import

Source: NYC Open Data, NYPD Shooting Incident Data (Historic), dataset ID 833y-fsy8.

The question this report asks: New York’s shooting volume moved dramatically over this period. Did the nature of those shootings change alongside the count — and what, if anything, predicts whether a shooting kills someone?

url_in <- "https://data.cityofnewyork.us/api/views/833y-fsy8/rows.csv?accessType=DOWNLOAD"

nypd_raw <- read_csv(url_in)

dim(nypd_raw)
## [1] 29744    21

The raw file has 29744 rows and 21 columns.

glimpse(nypd_raw)

One row is one victim, not one incident

INCIDENT_KEY is not unique meaning that when a shooting has more than one victim, a row (victim) will be created and incident key repeats. As every count in this report is a victim, reporting these as “incidents” would overstate the number of shooting events. Refer to below:

tibble(
  victim_rows      = nrow(nypd_raw),
  unique_incidents = n_distinct(nypd_raw$INCIDENT_KEY),
  multi_victim_pct = percent(1 - n_distinct(nypd_raw$INCIDENT_KEY) / nrow(nypd_raw),
                             accuracy = 0.1)
)
## # A tibble: 1 × 3
##   victim_rows unique_incidents multi_victim_pct
##         <int>            <int> <chr>           
## 1       29744            23298 21.7%

Missing data and common dirty data caused by data-entry errors

The Clean Up

Things that I cleaned up to make the dataset more reasonable and analyzable including time of the date without changing the meaning of any rows:

  1. Change OCCUR_DATE to a real date, and a derived OCCUR_HOUR so time of day can be analysed numerically.
  2. Mixed unknown values input unified to NA. "UNKNOWN" and "(null)" mean the same thing as a blank which should be counted as missing.
  3. Invalid age values dropped to NA. Keep unreasonable ‘noise’ out.
  4. Geographic coordinate columns removed. This analysis works at borough level, so point coordinates add nothing.
  5. LOC_OF_OCCUR_DESC and LOC_CLASSFCTN_DESC removed. These two columns are empty for the large majority of the record — see the check below. Keeping them would restrict analysis that used them to recent years only.
nypd_raw %>%
  mutate(yr = year(mdy(OCCUR_DATE))) %>%
  group_by(yr) %>%
  summarise(rows = n(),
            missing_loc_class = sum(is.na(LOC_CLASSFCTN_DESC)),
            pct_missing = percent(missing_loc_class / rows)) %>%
  print(n = Inf)
## # A tibble: 19 × 4
##       yr  rows missing_loc_class pct_missing
##    <dbl> <int>             <int> <chr>      
##  1  2006  2055              2055 100%       
##  2  2007  1887              1887 100%       
##  3  2008  1959              1959 100%       
##  4  2009  1828              1828 100%       
##  5  2010  1912              1912 100%       
##  6  2011  1939              1939 100%       
##  7  2012  1717              1717 100%       
##  8  2013  1339              1339 100%       
##  9  2014  1464              1464 100%       
## 10  2015  1434              1434 100%       
## 11  2016  1208              1208 100%       
## 12  2017   970               970 100%       
## 13  2018   958               958 100%       
## 14  2019   967               967 100%

valid_ages <- c("<18", "18-24", "25-44", "45-64", "65+")

cat_cols <- c("BORO", "PRECINCT", "JURISDICTION_CODE", "LOCATION_DESC",
              "PERP_SEX", "PERP_RACE", "VIC_SEX", "VIC_RACE")

nypd <- nypd_raw %>%
  mutate(OCCUR_DATE = mdy(OCCUR_DATE),
         OCCUR_HOUR = hour(OCCUR_TIME),
         YEAR       = year(OCCUR_DATE)) %>%
  # mixed unknown values inputs -> NA
  mutate(across(where(is.character),
                ~ if_else(.x %in% c("(null)", "UNKNOWN", "NONE"),
                          NA_character_, .x))) %>%
  mutate(across(c(PERP_SEX, VIC_SEX), ~ na_if(.x, "U"))) %>%
  # invalid age -> NA
  mutate(PERP_AGE_GROUP = factor(if_else(PERP_AGE_GROUP %in% valid_ages,
                                         PERP_AGE_GROUP, NA_character_),
                                 levels = valid_ages),
         VIC_AGE_GROUP  = factor(if_else(VIC_AGE_GROUP %in% valid_ages,
                                         VIC_AGE_GROUP, NA_character_),
                                 levels = valid_ages)) %>%
  mutate(across(any_of(cat_cols), factor)) %>%
  select(-any_of(c("X_COORD_CD", "Y_COORD_CD", "Latitude", "Longitude",
                   "Lon_Lat", "LOC_OF_OCCUR_DESC", "LOC_CLASSFCTN_DESC")))

Age brackets are set as ordered factor levels.

For the missing data

Column group Missing Treatment
Victim fields Very low Left as-is; negligible effect
JURISDICTION_CODE 2 rows Left as-is
LOCATION_DESC High Not used in the analysis below
Perpetrator fields ~45% Rows kept. Treated as a finding, not a defect — see Bias

Rows are not dropped. Deleting incomplete or dirty records would drop almost half the data and would increase bias.

Step 3: Visualize and Analyze

Finding 1: Volume changed drastically and then boroughs diverged

by_year_boro <- nypd %>% count(YEAR, BORO)

ggplot(by_year_boro, aes(YEAR, n, color = BORO)) +
  geom_line(linewidth = 0.9) +
  geom_point(size = 1.6) +
  scale_x_continuous(breaks = seq(2006, 2030, 2)) +
  labs(title    = "Shooting victims per year by borough",
       x = NULL, y = "Victims", color = "Borough") +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 12) +
  theme(plot.title = element_text(face = "bold"))

totals <- nypd %>% count(YEAR, name = "victims")

peak_year   <- totals %>% slice_max(victims, n = 1)
trough_year <- totals %>% filter(YEAR < 2020) %>% slice_min(victims, n = 1)
spike_2020  <- totals %>% filter(YEAR %in% c(2019, 2020))

totals %>% print(n = Inf)

Shooting volume fell steadily through the 2010s and hit a low of 958 victims in 2018, then rose radpidly in 2020 with an increase of 101% in one year. Every borough rose in 2020.

After the peak:

latest_yr <- max(nypd$YEAR)

recovery <- nypd %>%
  filter(YEAR %in% c(2019, latest_yr)) %>%
  mutate(period = if_else(YEAR == 2019, "pre", "latest")) %>%
  count(BORO, period) %>%
  pivot_wider(names_from = period, values_from = n) %>%
  mutate(change_vs_2019 = percent(latest / pre - 1, accuracy = 1)) %>%
  arrange(desc(latest / pre))
recovery
## # A tibble: 5 × 4

## 2 MANHATTAN        215   146 47%           
## 3 QUEENS           155   156 -1%           
## 4 BROOKLYN         339   372 -9%           
## 5 STATEN ISLAND     15    26 -42%
# years in which the Bronx recorded more victims than Brooklyn
nypd %>%
  filter(BORO %in% c("BRONX", "BROOKLYN")) %>%
  count(YEAR, BORO) %>%
  pivot_wider(names_from = BORO, values_from = n) %>%
  filter(BRONX > BROOKLYN)
## # A tibble: 3 × 3
##    YEAR BRONX BROOKLYN
##   <dbl> <int>    <int>
## 1  2021   701      631
## 2  2023   439      413
## 3  2024   458      339

By 2024, some boroughs were back at or below their 2019 level. The Bronx recorded more shooting victims than Brooklyn in several recent years even with its less dense population.

Finding 2: Volume and fatality run in opposite directions across the day

by_hour <- nypd %>%
  group_by(OCCUR_HOUR) %>%
  summarise(victims = n(),
            deaths  = sum(STATISTICAL_MURDER_FLAG),
            rate    = deaths / victims)

by_hour %>%
  select(OCCUR_HOUR, victims, rate) %>%
  pivot_longer(c(victims, rate)) %>%
  mutate(name = recode(name,
                       victims = "Victims (count)",
                       rate    = "Share fatal")) %>%
  ggplot(aes(OCCUR_HOUR, value)) +
  geom_line(linewidth = 0.9, color = "#2F4858") +
  geom_point(size = 1.6, color = "#2F4858") +
  facet_wrap(~name, scales = "free_y", ncol = 1) +
  scale_x_continuous(breaks = seq(0, 23, 3)) +
  labs(title    = "More shootings during the night. More dealy during the day.",
       x = "Hour of day", y = NULL,
       caption  = "Source: NYC Open Data 833y-fsy8") +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 12) +
  theme(plot.title = element_text(face = "bold"))

by_hour %>% mutate(rate = percent(rate, accuracy = 0.1)) %>% print(n = Inf)

hour_cor <- cor.test(by_hour$victims, by_hour$rate)
hour_cor
## 
##  Pearson's product-moment correlation
## 
## data:  by_hour$victims and by_hour$rate
## t = -5.3675, df = 22, p-value = 2.174e-05
## alternative hypothesis: true correlation is not equal to 0
## 95 percent confidence interval:
##  -0.8869730 -0.5021318
## sample estimates:
##        cor 
## -0.7530018
band_levels <- c("Late night (00-04)", "Morning (05-11)",
                 "Afternoon (12-17)", "Evening (18-23)")

nypd <- nypd %>%
  mutate(TIME_BAND = factor(case_when(
    OCCUR_HOUR <= 4  ~ band_levels[1],
    OCCUR_HOUR <= 11 ~ band_levels[2],
    OCCUR_HOUR <= 17 ~ band_levels[3],
    TRUE             ~ band_levels[4]), levels = band_levels))

by_band <- nypd %>%
  group_by(TIME_BAND) %>%
  summarise(victims = n(),
            deaths  = sum(STATISTICAL_MURDER_FLAG),
            rate    = deaths / victims)
by_band %>% mutate(rate = percent(rate, accuracy = 0.1))
## # A tibble: 4 × 4
##   TIME_BAND          victims deaths rate 
##   <fct>                <int>  <int> <chr>
## 1 Late night (00-04)    9741   1754 18.0%
## 2 Morning (05-11)       2725    676 24.8%
## 3 Afternoon (12-17)     5439   1071 19.7%
## 4 Evening (18-23)      11839   2264 19.1%
morning_rate <- by_band$rate[by_band$TIME_BAND == "Morning (05-11)"]
rest_rate <- nypd %>%
  filter(TIME_BAND != "Morning (05-11)") %>%
  summarise(r = mean(STATISTICAL_MURDER_FLAG)) %>% pull(r)

morning_test <- with(nypd, chisq.test(table(TIME_BAND == "Morning (05-11)",
                                            STATISTICAL_MURDER_FLAG)))
morning_test
## 
##  Pearson's Chi-squared test with Yates' continuity correction
## 
## data:  table(TIME_BAND == "Morning (05-11)", STATISTICAL_MURDER_FLAG)
## X-squared = 56.126, df = 1, p-value = 6.796e-14

Volume peaks late at night: the busiest hour has 9.7 times as many victims as the quietest. The fatality rate runs the opposite way. The correlation between hourly volume and hourly fatality rate is -0.75 (p = 2.2^{-5}).

Aggregating 05:00 to 11:59, morning shootings are fatal 24.8% of the time, against 18.8% for the rest of the day, a ratio of 1.32

This observation make me wonder why. Is it fewer bystanders to help, different kinds of shootings, or traffic during traffic peak hours blocking successful rescue? The model below tests the last of these.

Step 4: Bias and Conclusion

Counts are not rates. Brooklyn leads every volume chart in this report, and Brooklyn is also the most populous borough. Without population denominators these charts partly measure borough size.

nypd %>%
  count(BORO, sort = TRUE) %>%
  mutate(share = percent(n / sum(n), accuracy = 0.1))
## # A tibble: 5 × 3
##   BORO              n share
##   <fct>         <int> <chr>
## 1 BROOKLYN      11685 39.3%
## 2 BRONX          8834 29.7%
## 3 QUEENS         4426 14.9%
## 4 MANHATTAN      3977 13.4%
## 5 STATEN ISLAND   822 2.8%

Joining NYC population estimates would convert these to per-capita rates and could reorder the boroughs substantially. That join is the obvious next step and is deliberately left as an open question rather than papered over.

The outcome variable is not purely about violence. Whether a victim dies depends in part on how quickly they reach ER. STATISTICAL_MURDER_FLAG therefore blends the severity of the shooting with the quality and proximity of emergency medical care — a confound sitting inside the dependent variable itself.

This is police-recorded data. It captures shootings the NYPD recorded. Anything not reported to or recorded by the police is absent by construction, and reporting propensity is unlikely to be uniform across neighbourhoods.

Conclusion

New York’s shooting volume fell by more than half over the 2010s and then roughly doubled in 2020. Every borough rose together, but they did not come down together: by 2024 some had returned to their 2019 levels while the Bronx and Manhattan remained well above them.

Across the day the relationship is not just absent but reversed: lethality peaks in the morning, when shootings are rarest. Victim age is the strongest predictor of a fatal outcome.

The practical reading is that “how many shootings happen” and “how many shootings kill” are two different questions with two different sets of causes, and interventions aimed at one should not be expected to move the other.
